This is the third in a series by Paul Ong, Jonathan Ong, Sonja Diaz, and Melissa Chinchilla at UCLA's Center for Neighborhood Knowledge. All three briefs use the same Deportation Data Project FOIA dataset.

Self-deportation among detainees also surged, from fewer than 1 in 100 in early weeks to over 1 in 10 by September 2025. The brief is careful to note the data on voluntary departures outside ICE custody is still limited.

Speed increased too. Post-Miller, 1 in 4 arrestees was deported within a week of arrest, up from 1 in 5 before. The brief documents this as a deliberate curtailment of due process, not just administrative efficiency.

The "worst of the worst" share of Latino deportees fell from about 1-in-3 in early weeks to about 1-in-8 by September 2025. Meanwhile, noncriminals, people whose only violation was being undocumented, grew from 1-in-5 to 1-in-3 deportees.

ICE made over 187,000 Latino arrests in that nine-month window. Weekly deportations more than doubled, from roughly 2,000 per week to over 4,600, after Stephen Miller pushed for 3,000 arrests per day starting June 2025.

Latinos comprised 91% of noncitizen arrests from Jan–Oct 2025, despite making up 76–80% of the undocumented population. They accounted for 96% of Trump-era ICE arrestees subsequently deported. Source: UCLA CNK analysis of ICE FOIA data.

Senate Democrats had conditioned their votes on reforms to ICE following the January deaths of two U.S. citizens during federal enforcement operations in Minnesota. The final bill did not include those reforms. ICE and CBP will be funded separately through reconciliation.

That's an important data point. The shutdown was real and caused hardship for roughly 260,000 DHS employees. But it did not stop immigration enforcement operations in the way a full DHS shutdown would have. The enforcement data didn't pause, it kept accumulating.

The bill funds most of DHS (TSA, FEMA, the Coast Guard) but does not include ICE or CBP. Those agencies have separate funding streams, including from the 2025 reconciliation bill, which kept their enforcement operations largely running throughout the shutdown.

The DHS partial government shutdown that began February 14 ended April 30 (75 days) when Congress passed and Trump signed a bipartisan funding bill. That's the longest agency shutdown in U.S. history. It's worth understanding what it did and didn't affect.

Nagel's key insight: mass deportations like Operation Wetback (1954–55) and Depression-era expulsions of 2 million people of Mexican origin didn't reduce labor dependence on Mexican workers.

Stephen Miller's agenda is more radical than standard Republican restrictionism. Conservative pro-business politics have long supported H1B visas, 85,000 three-year visas/year for credentialed workers. Miller wants to gut that too.

 My broader analysis of ICE detention trends and the data behind them is at austinkocher.substack.com

His case illustrates something the detention data can't fully capture: the procedural mechanisms ICE uses to keep people detained even after judicial release orders. A judge granted bond. ICE placed a stay. A second judge then denied relief. That's three separate decision points.

A lawsuit ultimately led to his release in early May 2026. Rep. Dan Goldman (D-NY) said 30 other people were released alongside Marrero through his office's triage center. Marrero's attorney is from Make the Road New York.

The original detention stemmed from a removal order issued in 2022 after Marrero missed a court date while in a rehabilitation program for alcohol addiction. Attorneys describe a missed court date during medical treatment as legally recognized "good cause" for non-appearance.

He was transferred through at least 5 detention facilities: New Jersey, Arizona, Texas, the Everglades facility known as "Alligator Alcatraz," and finally Mississippi. He described being shackled at the ankles, waist, and wrists for up to 8 hours during transfers.

Allan Michael Marrero spent 150 days in ICE detention after being seized at a routine marriage-based green card interview at 26 Federal Plaza in NYC last November. He has no criminal history. A judge ordered his release in January. ICE stayed the order and kept him locked up.

Trump vowed to fight crime in Minneapolis. Prosecutions plunged.
